title: What Costs Rows and Proving Time in Small EZKL Transformer Circuits, and What It Costs in Perplexity
abstract: Design advice for zero-knowledge (ZK) transformer inference rests on analytical constraint-count models and on swapping activations for cheaper ones. We test an analytical model against EZKL 23.0.5 on small causal transformers and measure what each choice costs in perplexity. We compile 108 configurations (width 64–128, 1–4 layers, sequence length 8–32, four activation variants) and generate 24 verified proofs. The analytical model ranks compiled row counts well (Spearman $`\rho{=}0.93`$) but no better than the product of the dimensions ($`0.96`$), is uncalibrated (measured/modelled rows $`0.12`$–$`0.53`$), and predicts held-out widths, depths and sequence lengths worse ($`24`$–$`38\%`$ error) than a power law ($`6`$–$`18\%`$) or a calibrated additive model ($`8`$–$`11\%`$). On 16 out-of-range configurations (width 256–512) the analytical model’s fitted prediction errs by $`122\%`$ against $`10\%`$ for the dimension product, and the activation overheads persist (GELU $`1.45`$–$`1.54\times`$, ReLU $`1.08`$–$`1.17\times`$ the linear variant’s rows). Rows predict proving time (Spearman $`0.89`$ over six shapes, no better than the dimension product), and proving time is a step function of the power-of-two proving domain: crossing a boundary doubled it. Repeated runs on a shared machine differ by up to $`1.9\times`$, so proving times do not separate the nonlinearities. For sequences up to 32, the FFN nonlinearity dominates the row overhead for GELU and poly2 (at width 128, ReLU $`+7\%`$, poly2 $`+20\%`$, GELU $`+42\%`$), but softmax grows with sequence length (from $`4\%`$ to $`24\%`$ at width 64 as the length goes from 8 to 64). EZKL’s domain size also depends on an implementation detail, the causal-mask fill value, which moved it from 19 to 26 at constant rows. In a WikiText-2 study (3 seeds, validation-selected checkpoints), ReLU, poly2 and GELU are within $`1\%`$ in perplexity, larger models help, and nothing trained from scratch approaches pretrained GPT-2. Compiled circuits reach width 512 (the grid width 128) with at most four layers, proofs only domains up to $`2^{21}`$, proving times come from one or two runs on a shared machine, and quantized accuracy is not measured. Code and raw records are released.
